subject: Architecture
title: Teotihuacán: The City of Gods
description: A quick, practical guide to Teotihuacán: The City of Gods.

hook.text: Teotihuacán was the largest city in the Americas in 100 AD — home to 125,000 people in planned neighborhoods.

buildup.text: The Avenue of the Dead runs two miles through the city, lined with platforms, temples, and pyramids.

discovery.text: The Pyramid of the Sun is the third-largest pyramid on Earth — built with three million tons of material.

twist.text: Nobody knows who built it. The Aztecs arrived 700 years later and named it — they were just as mystified.

climax.text: Recent tunnel excavations found mercury pools, jade figures, and seashells deep under the pyramids.

punchline.text: The city that dwarfed Rome. Built by people whose name we still don't know.

quiz.question: Who originally built Teotihuacán?
options: Unknown — the builders' identity remains a mystery

details.summary: Teotihuacán in central Mexico was one of the largest cities in the ancient world, with a population of 125,000 at its peak around 450 CE. Its Avenue of the Dead, Pyramid of the Sun, and Pyramid of the Moon were built by an unknown civilization that left no written records behind.
details.whyItMatters: Teotihuacán challenges assumptions about urbanism — a city this size existed without a known writing system or identifiable ruling dynasty. Its careful urban planning rivals contemporary Rome in sophistication.
takeaways: Teotihuacán peaked at 125,000 people around 450 CE
The builders left no written records of their civilization
Its urban planning rivaled contemporary Rome in scale

faq.question: Who built Teotihuacán?
faq.answer: Nobody knows for certain. The city was already ancient and abandoned when the Aztecs found it. Its builders left no writing that has been deciphered. The name Teotihuacán is Aztec, meaning 'place where the gods were born,' reflecting their awe at the ruins.

faq.question: How big is the Pyramid of the Sun?
faq.answer: It stands 65 meters tall with a base of 225 meters per side — roughly the same base area as the Great Pyramid at Giza. It contains an estimated 1.2 million cubic meters of material and was the third-largest pyramid in the ancient world by volume.
